title: String
body:
Text. C++ has two kinds and the course uses both, which is the confusing part.

| | [[C-String]] | `string` |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | `char` [[Array]] ending in `'\0'` | a [[Class]] from the standard library |
| Needs | nothing | `#include <string>` |
| Size | fixed at compile time | grows as needed |
| Compare | `strcmp(a, b)` | `a == b` |
| Join | `strcat`, carefully | `a + b` |
| Length | `strlen(s)`, not counting `'\0'` | `s.length()` |

```c++
char old_way[6] = "Hello";     // 6 slots for 5 characters
string new_way = "Hello";      // no size to get wrong
```

A `string` is not an [[Atomic type]]; it is a class, which makes it the course's first
working example of an [[Abstract Data Type]] you use without knowing how it works. The
C-string is what it is built out of, and it is where the null terminator, the off-by-one
size, and the lack of bounds checking all live.

Reading them differs too: `cin >> s` stops at whitespace, `getline(cin, s)` takes the whole
line. Mixing the two is the classic [[Buffered Input]] problem.
